newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - President Iliescu no sure bet in Romanian election.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - President Iliescu no sure bet in Romanian election.

text.p: President Ion Iliescu, who has led Romania since the 1989 fall of communism, is seeking four more years in power in Sunday's election but widespread misery and a changing national mood make him far from a sure bet.
Iliescu has won twice previously at the ballot box.

He coasted to victory with 85 percent of the vote in 1990 in the euphoria that followed the overthrow of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu and handily defeated five rivals in 1992, portraying himself as the "father of the nation".

But as living standards fall ever faster behind those in Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- the countries to which Romanians like to compare themselves -- the former communist is finding the going considerably tougher.

"It's hard to create a new society after communism," he told a rally last week. "We must eliminate the elements which create tension. Join our forces to create a better country. We have to work to create prosperity."
Iliescu's message that he is the guarantor of stability in comparison with Romania's sometimes unruly neighbours is clearly not always getting across.
Stocky and often sporting a workers' style cap or denim shirt while on the rural campaign trail, Iliescu still leads 15 other candidates in Romania's erratic opinion polls.

But the latest survey by Romania's most reliable opinion institute showed a seven-point lead reduced to just three over academic Emil Constantinescu -- the man he beat in 1992. A run-off round is virtually certain.

Iliescu's vast political machine -- the Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) -- lies second behind Constantinescu's Democratic Convention (CDR) in polls for parliamentary elections also being held on Sunday.
Even if he hangs on for a third victory, Iliescu will have to deal with a coalition government and a parliament less amenable towards him.
Voters in rural heartlands which once provided the bedrock of his support have given him a polite reception, but no more.

In cities hit by economic decline, crowds have sometimes been downright hostile. Iliescu had to be ushered from the back door of a hall in the southern town of Craiova to avoid jeering students. He was confronted by workers at a tractor plant in Brasov demanding an end to "humbug".
The opposition, better organised and more sophisticated than four years ago, hammers home the message of mass poverty and lost opportunities with reforms.

Both Constantinescu and Petre Roman, Romania's first post-communist prime minister, call for faster change likely to cause even more initial pain before the long-awaited upturn -- though they spend much of their time attacking each other.
Constantinescu's CDR has drafted a "contract" with voters modelled on the U.S. Republican Party pledging to resign if it fails to implement reforms within a strict time frame.
Its posters plastered in towns and villages show a loaf of bread costing three lei in in 1990 and 500 lei six years later.

Impeccably dressed and temples now greying, Roman was thrown out of office after hardline miners rampaged through Bucharest in 1991 to denounce his liberal economic policies -- at Iliescu's behest, he says.
Roman, third in the polls, says 4.5 million people live in poverty and points to average monthly incomes of about $80 -- down from $130 in 1991 and a third of those in Poland.
"The people who conducted reforms in 1992 could not keep their promises. People are tired of corruption and injustice," he told a a television interviewer.
"Since 1992, reforms have become bogged down. The president speaks of reforms but they are not working."
Pledges by all sides to hold a gentlemanly campaign fell by the wayside, with underhanded jibes and widespread allegations that Iliescu and the PDSR were plotting to rig the outcome.

Iliescu's television spots portrayed Constantinescu as a closet monarchist -- a vote loser in what has become a solidly republican country -- and all but denounced Roman as a criminal who plundered state coffers.
Constantinescu's clips unsubtly juxtaposed Iliescu with Ceausescu engaged in a communist-era harangue.
With a week to go in the campaign, opposition parties set aside differences and forged a tactical alliance against what they contend is a masterplan by the PDSR to alter the outcome.
There has been no shortage of intrigue.
Journalists raided the offices of an institute linked to the PDSR which had been conducting a telephone poll with questions clearly loaded against Iliescu's opponents.

A plan by election officials to allow voters to produce either identity papers or electors' cards to cast ballots was denounced -- and abandoned -- as being open to abuse. The number of eligible voters on lists oscillated from 15 to 17 million.
Opposition politicians complained that PDSR officials were appointed returning officers at polling stations in flagrant breach of election rules.
But the opposition pact is clearly temporary and does not extend to post-election coalition negotiations.
Iliescu says he is ready to cooperate with any group willing to work with him. Both main opposition parties say they will have nothing to do with the ruling PDSR.
Commentators say calls by Iliescu and others for a grand coalition are unrealistic.

"The relations are such between the main parties that I cannot see any cooperation with the PDSR," said Vladimir Pasti of the think tank "A Future for Romania". "Cooperation with the PDSR is possible only after a new government collapses." ($1=3363 Lei)
